title.analysis: Authentic title "The 50 Year Mortgage Trap That'll Keep You in Debt Forever" is a warning frame tied to a live policy idea. The script delivers it with amortization arithmetic and a supply-side argument; "forever" is hyperbole for a 50-year term.

script.stored_text_completeness: All 19685 canonical characters read sequentially in full in 1 bounded ranges; auto-generated untimed text; stored text ends on a slogan ("Don't let them turn the American dream into a generational nightmare.") with no sign-off; filler ("um", "U Warren Buffett", "pres on") and a "[snorts]" marker; the $400,000 "home" is treated as a $400,000 loan with no down payment; audio, timed delivery and editing unverified.
script.opening_words: What if I told you that America's newest housing solution could turn your mortgage into a lifelong prison sentence? What if the very policy designed to help you buy a home could actually guarantee you'll never truly own it? My name is Nick and I've spent years helping people understand how money really works. Today, we need to talk about something that could fundamentally change home ownership in America forever. We're talking about 50-year mortgages. And if you think this
script.ending_words: isn't solving the housing crisis. It's making it worse while pretending to help. You're not getting a better deal. You're getting a longer prison sentence with better marketing. The math doesn't lie. Even when politicians do. Uh if you can't afford a 30-year mortgage, a 50-year mortgage won't save you. It'll just make your financial problems someone else's inheritance. Don't let them turn the American dream into a generational nightmare.
script.analysis: Full 19685 canonical characters read. A single-narrator opinion explainer reacting to the November 2025 50-year mortgage idea: hook, amortization comparison, compound-interest framing, a Japan cautionary tale, payment bias, supply as the real fix, slow equity building, retirement and Social Security, inheritance, induced demand, industry and political motives, life-event risks, Houston vs San Francisco, and a slogan close. The core arithmetic reproduces; the Japan history, the "exactly" induced-demand claim, the industry-support claim and the San Francisco aside are unsupported, and the proposer is never named.
beat_map: Life events: job loss, divorce, elder care.

claim_audit.claim: Japan introduced 50-year mortgages in the 1990s as a fix; its market collapsed 70% and took 36 years to recover.
claim_audit.stored_text_witness:

claim_audit.assessment: Inaccurate history: long-term and multi-generation mortgages appeared during the late-1980s bubble, not as a 1990s response; big-city land prices fell sharply (on the order of 70%+ in commercial land) but most Japanese land prices have not regained 1991 peaks, and the Nikkei took about 34 years (1989 to 2024). The script itself concedes the mortgages were not the main cause.
